question: The EU is facing hybrid threats, migration pressures, organised crime and persistent rule-oflaw challenges. Several candidate countries in the Western Balkans are themselves affected by foreign interference. The Commission has acknowledged that a larger EU could require additional resources, complicate decision-making and produce unintended consequences1. Against this background: 1.
Does the Commission consider that further accession negotiations with candidate countries in the Western Balkans should be suspended for at least 10 years?

If not, what objective evidence supports the Commission’s assessment that the EU currently has the institutional, financial and security capacity to admit additional Member States without weakening its internal stability, border management or ability to take decisions?

Under what security-related circumstances would the Commission recommend the suspension or reversal of accession negotiations, particularly where a candidate country does not exercise effective control over its territory or borders or is particularly vulnerable to foreign interference and organised crime?
Commission communication of 20 March 2024 on pre-enlargement reforms and policy reviews (COM(2024)0146). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.11.2026) Member States have repeatedly affirmed their support for the European perspective of the Western Balkans. In the Granada Declaration of October 20231, the Heads of State or Government recognised enlargement as a geostrategic investment in peace, security, stability and prosperity.

Furthermore, in its Conclusions of 18 and 19 June 20262, the European Council reiterated that the EU will continue to work closely with Western Balkans partners and support their reform efforts on their respective paths towards EU membership. Demonstrating sustained results in fighting against organised crime and in effectively managing borders is key for candidate countries to progress on their EU accession path.

These feature among the so-called ‘Fundamentals’ of the accession process. Under the 2020 revised enlargement methodology, progress in these areas determines the overall pace of negotiations. To prevent stagnation or backsliding, chapters under the Fundamentals cluster are the last to be closed before concluding the accession negotiations.

The Commission has several tools in place, from regular policy dialogues and reporting to expert missions, peer-review assessments, technical assistance initiatives and contacts with relevant EU Justice and Home Affairs agencies, which also monitor security risks in candidate countries and potential candidates.

The capacity of the EU to absorb new members has been a consideration since the Copenhagen European Council of 1993. To be prepared for a larger Union and to understand its impact on governance, policies and budget, the Commission adopted the Communication on Preparing for a wider Union on 6 October 20263.
Gradual integration and safeguards featured prominently in this Communication, as means of reconciling the opportunities of a larger Union with the challenges it poses.
